title: CRAG: Can 3D Generative Models Help 3D Assembly?
claim: Two coupled branches exchange information through a shared adapter, so solving structure and whole-shape synthesis jointly beats treating them separately.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; (a) coupled architecture, (b) joint flow detail with dashed divider
description: Two-panel architecture figure separated by a dashed vertical line. Panel (a), Coupled Architecture, has two vertical stacks. On the left, fragments with a missing part go through a VAE backbone and an Assembly Branch (pink dashed box) to give an assembly result. On the right, an optional reference image goes through DINOv2 and a Generation Branch (gray dashed box) to give a generated chair. An orange double arrow labeled Interact links the two branches. Panel (b), Iteration with Joint Flow, zooms into the interaction. A top Generation Flow runs from a blue Gaussian noise latent to a gray generation latent along curved trajectories. A bottom Assembly Flow runs from a noise pose to a pink assembly latent. A middle dashed block holds Self Attn, Cross Attn, Global Attn and Bi-direction Cross Attn modules with colored cross arrows and a repeat-xM symbol. Pastel blue, yellow, green and pink fills guide the eye.
caption: Overview of our approach \acronym{} . We propose a unified framework for 3D assembly and whole-shape generation. Our model consists of two interacting branches: an Assembly Branch that predicts the pose for each part via SE(3) flow matching, and a Generation Branch that synthesizes the complete shape via flow matching. A Joint Adapter bridges these branches, enabling bidirectional information flow. We employ a two-stage training strategy: learning assembly first, and then jointly finetuning both tasks.
abstract: Most existing 3D assembly methods treat the problem as pure pose estimation, rearranging observed parts via rigid transformations. In contrast, human assembly naturally couples structural reasoning with holistic shape inference. Inspired by this intuition, we reformulate 3D assembly as a joint problem of assembly and generation. We show that these two processes are mutually reinforcing: assembly provides part-level structural priors for generation, while generation injects holistic shape context that resolves ambiguities in assembly. Unlike prior methods that cannot synthesize missing geometry, we propose CRAG, which simultaneously generates plausible complete shapes and predicts poses for input parts. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across in-the-wild objects with diverse geometries, varying part counts, and missing pieces.
